title: Switch a focused microscope to its 100x oil objective: nosepiece half-turned, one drop on the lit spot, 40x kept dry
instruction: Switch the microscope from the 40x objective to the 100x oil objective for the stained smear, put the oil dropper back in its bottle, and take both hands away.
context: Gram stains, blood smears and malaria films are read under a 100x oil-immersion objective in clinical, microbiology and teaching labs; a robot that reads slides must make this switch. The 40x front lens sits 0.6 mm above the slide, so oil put on under it, or the 40x turned back through the oil, fouls the lens. The oil has to go onto the lit spot through the gap the half-turned nosepiece leaves, with a squeeze that gives one drop, not a stream.
setup: Millimetres from the midpoint between the two arm bases (x forward, y to the robot's left); heights above the bench. Swift SW350B student compound microscope (fixed; painted cast-metal body, black anodized aluminium nosepiece ring, metal objective barrels; sizes other than its objectives are estimates): base 215 x 150 x 30, light path at (300, 0), stage 140 x 140 with its top 120 up and toward the robot, arm behind the light path, binocular head turned so its eyepieces face away (it turns 360 degrees), 404 tall. A stained smear on a 75 x 25 x 1 glass slide, long side left-right, in the stage's slide holder; the lit spot (4 across) is at the light path. Quadruple revolving nosepiece: knurled ring 72 across and 18 thick, its axis 28 behind the light path and leaning 15 degrees toward the robot, click stops every 90 degrees; objectives with coloured bands, shoulders 45 above the slide: 40x (blue, 0.6 working distance) in the light path, focused; 100x oil (white, 0.2) to the right; 4x (red, 17) at the back; 10x (yellow, 7) to the left. Kimble 30 mL glass dropping bottle with a 12/18 ground neck (DWK 15035-30, sold with ground-in pipet and bulb as Fisher 02992A; drawn amber; 36 across, neck top 88 up, 75 g, estimates) of Cargille Type A immersion oil at (205, -150), its glass dropper (114 long, 12 g; red rubber bulb 15 across and 32 long on top; estimates) seated in the 12/18 ground neck. Lot B: the bottle and dropper at (255, -190); the microscope is the same. Trials alternate A, B and are averaged; the screenshot shows lot A.
scoring: Read from a front camera looking 45 degrees down through the gap under the half-turned nosepiece at a 1 mm grid printed on clear film under the slide, the overhead and side videos, and a lens-paper wipe of the 40x after the trial. Score 0 for the whole trial if, at any moment: oil touches the 40x, 10x or 4x front lens (a drop put on under it, or the nosepiece turned so it passes through a drop); oil lands anywhere but the slide (on the stage, the bench or any objective; a drop falls straight down from the tip, and one released from below the slide's top or more than 25 mm above it counts as off the slide), more than two drops are put on, or the bulb is squeezed into a stream; a robot finger or the dropper touches an objective (any contact; simulation: over 0.1 N); or the oil bottle tips over (more than 45 degrees). Otherwise, with the bottle and dropper still (under 5 mm/s and 0.1 rad/s) and the nosepiece not turning (under 4 degrees a second) for the last 1 s: 0.25 one or two drops on the slide, the first one's centre within 3 mm of the centre of the lit spot (the front camera's frame when it lands, against the grid); 0.5 and the 100x is at its click stop in the light path (within 2 degrees; the nosepiece's index mark) with the drop under its front lens (front photo shows the oil bridging slide and lens); 0.75 and the dropper is home in its bottle (shoulder within 3 mm above the neck, centred within 2 mm, within 10 degrees of the bottle's axis) and the bottle stands (within 10 degrees of upright, base within 3 mm of the bench; side photo with a ruler); 1.0 and nothing is held, both hands at least 30 mm from the nosepiece, objectives, bottle and dropper for the last 1 s. Otherwise 0. Trials on lots A and B are averaged.
run_limit: 1,200 steps (60 s at 20 Hz) per trial; two trials (lots A and B)
reset_notes: The focus knobs are taped so the stage cannot move. 1. Wipe the slide's oil and the 100x front lens with lens paper and lens cleaner; check the 40x front lens is clean. 2. Turn the nosepiece back to the 40x click stop (the smear stays in focus at the taped stage height). 3. Seat the dropper in its bottle (bulb squeezed and released once in the oil so it is loaded) and stand the bottle on its lot's tape outline. 4. Fit fresh nitrile finger cots on the gripper pads if any oil reached them. 5. Both arms at their start pose. Run with -E object_jitter=0 and --epochs 2.
fidelity: Objective magnifications, slide and bottle from maker listings; microscope body, nosepiece, working distances, dropper sizes, masses and forces are estimates. No liquid: 10 N on both bulb pads, tip down, releases one 5 x 1.2 mm drop straight down from the tip; over 35 N squirts a stream. The ring is held by friction (1.0), knurling not modelled. The nosepiece holds about 0.016 N m and click stops pull it in within 10 degrees. Slide fixed; objective fronts rigid.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (lots A and B 0 each; both ran to the 1,200-step limit without refusing; the arms hovered and the right hand came near the stage but never took the dropper or turned the nosepiece); demo: 1.0 in each of lots A and B (full score at 28 s)
